name: The Yerkes-Dodson Law
statement: Performance rises with arousal to a peak, then falls — an inverted U.
meaning: In its popular form, performance improves as arousal or pressure increases, but only up to a point; past an optimal level, more arousal makes performance worse, tracing an inverted U. A second part holds that the best level of arousal is lower for hard or complex tasks and higher for simple, well-practised ones. Some pressure sharpens; too much impairs.
mechanism: The proposed explanation is attentional: rising arousal narrows the range of cues a person attends to, first filtering out distractions helpfully, then, as it climbs further, excluding cues the task actually needs. A parallel physiological story runs through stress hormones, whose effect on memory follows its own inverted U, moderate levels aiding consolidation and both very low and very high levels impairing it. Both accounts are ways of dressing the curve in a mechanism; neither settles that the general law holds.

examples.text: A little exam nerves can sharpen performance, while overwhelming anxiety impairs recall — the canonical illustration of the inverted U.
An athlete performs best when optimally aroused and worse when over-aroused and choking, with fine-skill tasks tolerating less arousal than raw power tasks.
Yerkes and Dodson found that mice learned a hard discrimination fastest under mild electric shock but a simple one under stronger shock — the difficulty-dependence at the law's root.

variants.name: The difficulty-dependence
variants.text: The better-supported half: that the optimal level of arousal or motivation falls as a task grows harder, which the original mouse experiments actually showed.

variants.name: Hebb's arousal curve
variants.text: The general arousal-performance inverted U, proposed by Donald Hebb in the 1950s and often attributed to the 1908 study, though the original never measured arousal or a general performance.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most cited ideas in popular psychology, invoked across education, sport, management, and stress research to explain why some pressure helps and too much hurts. Its tangled history is just as instructive: it shows how a memorable curve can be read back into an old experiment that never drew it, a caution about the gap between a finding and its folklore.

working.text: seek a middling level of arousal for demanding work, since too little and too much both tend to impair.
allow higher arousal for simple, well-learned tasks and lower for complex ones, the part of the law with the firmer basis.
treat the universal inverted U as a contested generalisation rather than an established law, especially for humans.

limits: The law is contested. Its central term, arousal, is a catch-all spanning activation, drive, stress, and effort, often unmeasured, which makes the claim hard to test and hard to falsify, since any null result can be explained as arousal not pushed far enough. Human evidence for the smooth inverted U is surprisingly thin, with many studies finding simply that more stress worsens performance. Its historical basis is thinner than its ubiquity suggests: tiny mouse samples, a curvilinearity that depended on how learning was measured, and an inverted U that originated with Hebb in the 1950s, not the 1908 authors. The difficulty-dependence has genuine support; the universal curve does not.
misreadings: Yerkes and Dodson did not discover or draw the arousal-performance inverted U — they studied shock strength, task difficulty, and habit formation in mice, and the famous smooth curve and the word arousal are later constructions, chiefly Hebb's. The clean textbook graph is not the original 1908 figure. And arousal is not a single well-defined variable, which is part of why the law resists rigorous test.
origin: Rooted in Robert Yerkes and John Dillingham Dodson's 1908 experiments on mice learning under electric shock, which showed the optimal stimulus falling with task difficulty; the general arousal-performance inverted U was proposed by Donald Hebb in the 1950s and retrospectively attached to their names.

sources.text: Yerkes & Dodson, "The Relation of Strength of Stimulus to Rapidity of Habit-Formation," Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology 18:459-482 (1908), York University Classics. — the original difficulty-dependent result in mice.

Nieuwenhuis, "Arousal and performance: revisiting the famous inverted-U-shaped curve," Trends in Cognitive Sciences 28(5):394-396 (2024). — the reinterpretation history and the case that the curve is Hebb's, not the 1908 authors'.
"Yerkes-Dodson: Lore, not Law," The Learning Scientists (2024). — the weak human evidence and the myth framing.
